risk_rules.likely_cause: Battery terminal corrosion has damaged the keypad or control board. Intermittent electronic failure indicates imminent lockout.
risk_rules.technician_notes: Test voltage at battery contacts. Inspect PCB for corrosion wicking. If unit powers but fails sporadically, replace keypad assembly. For LaGard/ILS models, check ribbon connector.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Replace battery contacts and keypad assembly. Clean terminals. Test full cycle 10x before closing door.
risk_rules.parts_tools: Replacement keypad assembly, battery contacts, contact cleaner (DeoxIT D5), multimeter, small flathead, 1.5mm hex, sacrificial batteries
risk_rules.customer_explanation: The battery area has corrosion that is damaging the electronics. It may stop working entirely at any moment. Replacing the keypad and battery contacts now will prevent a lockout.

risk_rules.likely_cause: Dried or contaminated lubricant in the lock case combined with worn wheel pack bearings. Dial drag of 2+ inch-pounds indicates imminent failure.
risk_rules.technician_notes: Check dial torque with inch-pound gauge. Listen for grinding. Remove lock case and inspect wheel pack bushings. S&G 6730/6735 bearing failures common after 20 yrs.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Remove lock case, clean old lubricant, inspect wheel pack bushings, apply graphite or appropriate lubricant, reinstall and test. Replace bushings if worn.
risk_rules.parts_tools: Lock case removal tools, graphite powder (not oil), inch-pound torque gauge, replacement bushings (if S&G R-series or LaGard), inspection mirror
risk_rules.customer_explanation: The internal mechanism is dry and worn from years of use. It's getting harder to turn because the parts are binding. A professional cleaning and lubrication will restore smooth operation and prevent a future lockout.

risk_rules.likely_cause: Rust or debris in the bolt mechanism. High humidity environment accelerates corrosion on bolt slide surfaces.
risk_rules.technician_notes: Test bolt throw with door open. Inspect bolt slides for rust/pitting. Check linkage pins — dry pivot points are common. Pay attention to relock trigger area.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Clean and lubricate bolt slides and linkage. Wire-brush rust. Apply dry-film lubricant to sliding surfaces, light oil to pivots. Cycle door 20x.
risk_rules.parts_tools: Wire brush, dry-film lubricant (Tri-Flow or equivalent), light machine oil, rags, flashlight
risk_rules.customer_explanation: The bolts that lock the door are sticking because of moisture and lack of maintenance. Cleaning and lubricating them will make the handle operate smoothly again.

risk_rules.likely_cause: Door sag from foundation settling or hinge wear. Garage/outbuilding temperature swings cause expansion/contraction issues.
risk_rules.technician_notes: Check door gap top-to-bottom. Measure with feeler gauge. Check hinge pins for wear. Verify floor is level within 1/8". Check hinge bolts aren't loose.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Tighten hinge bolts. Shim if needed. Adjust strike plates. If door is out of square, note it for structural evaluation.
risk_rules.parts_tools: Socket set, feeler gauge, shim stock, level, torque wrench
risk_rules.customer_explanation: The door is slightly out of alignment, likely from the floor settling or temperature changes in your garage. Adjusting the hinges will fix the drag.

risk_rules.likely_cause: Low battery voltage under load or loose battery connections. Heavy daily use drains batteries faster than expected.
risk_rules.technician_notes: Test battery voltage under load (press keypad while metering). Check spring contacts. Many electronic locks beep but don't fire solenoid when voltage drops below 4.8V for 6V systems.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Replace batteries with fresh alkaline. Clean contacts. Test 5 cycles. Advise customer on annual battery replacement schedule.
risk_rules.parts_tools: Fresh alkaline batteries (correct size), multimeter, contact cleaner
risk_rules.customer_explanation: The batteries are getting weak and don't have enough power to reliably unlock the safe every time. Fresh batteries will fix this — I recommend changing them once a year.

risk_rules.likely_cause: Original factory lubrication has dried out. No immediate danger but will worsen over time.
risk_rules.technician_notes: Check dial torque. If below 2 in-lbs and operation is consistent, service is preventive. If not addressed within 12-18 months, may progress to mechanical seizure.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Open lock case, clean and regraphite. Check wheel pack and drive cam. Educate customer on symptoms of worsening condition.
risk_rules.parts_tools: Lock case tools, graphite powder, cleaning solvent, inspection light
risk_rules.customer_explanation: The internal lubricant has dried out over time. It's not urgent, but servicing it now will keep it operating smoothly for years. If you wait, it could eventually get hard to open.

risk_rules.likely_cause: Dial set-screw loosened or drive cam retaining ring working loose. Not immediately critical but can lead to inaccurate dialing.
risk_rules.technician_notes: Check set-screw on dial hub. Verify drive cam retaining ring is tight. For S&G dials, check that the spring washer is present under the dial.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Tighten set-screw or drive cam retaining ring. Test dial operation through full rotation.
risk_rules.parts_tools: Small flathead screwdriver, hex key set (usually 3/32 or 5/64 for set-screws), needle-nose pliers
risk_rules.customer_explanation: The dial has a small loose connection. It won't cause a lockout now, but if it gets worse, it could throw off your combination. A quick adjustment now will fix it.

risk_rules.likely_cause: Handle spindle or clutch mechanism has stripped or disengaged. This is a mechanical failure that prevents lock operation entirely.
risk_rules.technician_notes: With the door open, observe handle engagement. Check handle hub splines, clutch plate engagement (common on AMSEC and Gardall), and link arm connections to the bolt bar. The handle turning freely without engaging bolts indicates a broken spindle, stripped gear, or disengaged clutch.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Inspect and replace handle mechanism. Remove handle, check spindle splines and clutch assembly. Replace damaged parts. Test full throw cycle before closing.
risk_rules.parts_tools: Replacement handle assembly, clutch rebuild kit (AMSEC/Gardall), spline grease, snap-ring pliers, hex key set, socket set, replacement bolts if sheared
risk_rules.customer_explanation: The handle is spinning freely because an internal part has broken or stripped inside the lock mechanism. This requires immediate repair — the safe is currently inoperable and needs a technician.

risk_rules.likely_cause: No maintenance history. Risk factors unknown. Preventative inspection warranted regardless of current symptoms.
risk_rules.technician_notes: Perform full inspection: check lock case, bolt work, door alignment, hinge pins, relock device condition. Document all findings for baseline.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Complete preventive service: clean lock, lubricate bolts, verify combination, test all functions, inspect relock device.
risk_rules.parts_tools: Full service kit (lock tools, lubricants, cleaning supplies, replacement batteries, flashlight, inspection mirror)
risk_rules.customer_explanation: Your safe has never been serviced, and safes need regular maintenance just like cars. I'll do a full inspection to make sure everything is in good shape and catch any problems early.

risk_rules.likely_cause: Dial wear has caused the combination numbers to drift over time. The internal parts that align to the numbers are no longer reading correctly.
risk_rules.technician_notes: Test by trying combination +1 on each number, then -1. If this works, the dial has drifted. Dial must be serviced before safe is closed again. Clean and adjust wheel pack; check drive cam and fence alignment.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Remove and service the lock case. Clean wheel pack. Check drive cam for wear. Re-index dial ring or replace if worn. Verify combination before closing door.
risk_rules.parts_tools: Lock case removal tools, dial ring removal tool, replacement dial ring if worn, graphite powder, S&G/LaGard service manual
risk_rules.customer_explanation: The numbers on the dial no longer line up correctly due to wear over time. Adding one number to each digit may work temporarily, but the dial needs service or replacement to fix it permanently.

risk_rules.likely_cause: The setscrew securing the handle to the spindle has loosened over time, causing the handle to spin freely.
risk_rules.technician_notes: Check the hex setscrew at the base of the handle. Distinguish from a clutched handle: if the handle spins with very little resistance even when locked, it's a loose screw. A clutched handle requires significant force to spin.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Tighten the setscrew with the appropriate hex key. Use threadlocker (Loctite blue) if available. Test handle engagement through full cycle.
risk_rules.parts_tools: Hex key set (typically 3/32 or 5/64), Loctite 242 (blue), flashlight
risk_rules.customer_explanation: The handle has a small screw that holds it in place, and it has worked loose over time. Tightening it will restore normal operation.

risk_rules.likely_cause: Multiple incorrect code entries triggered the safe's security lockout feature. This is a built-in anti-hacking measure, not a mechanical failure.
risk_rules.technician_notes: Inform customer of lockout duration (varies by manufacturer, typically 1-5 minutes). If lockout lasts longer than expected, refer to manufacturer manual. Some models require a master code or physical key override.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Wait for the lockout timer to expire. Enter the correct code carefully. If lockout repeats, verify the correct code or check for keypad issues.
risk_rules.parts_tools: Manufacturer manual, possible master code documentation, no tools required
risk_rules.customer_explanation: The safe locked itself temporarily because the wrong code was entered too many times. This is a security feature. Wait a few minutes and try the correct code again carefully.

risk_rules.likely_cause: Internal door linkage connecting the handle to the bolt bars has broken, snapped, or come disconnected.
risk_rules.technician_notes: With door open (if possible), observe handle rotation vs bolt movement. Listen for loose metal inside door. Common on inexpensive safes with spot-welded linkages. Quality safes use bolted linkages.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Open the door (safe must already be open). Remove inner door panel. Inspect linkage connections. Replace broken linkage bar or reattach disconnected parts. Upgrade to bolted linkage if applicable.
risk_rules.parts_tools: Socket set, screwdrivers, replacement linkage bar, welder or bolts depending on safe type, panel removal tools
risk_rules.customer_explanation: The internal mechanism that connects the handle to the locking bolts has broken. This requires opening the door panel to repair. If the safe is locked closed, a technician must open it first.

risk_rules.likely_cause: Items inside the safe are pressing against the door or blocking the bolt holes, preventing bolts from retracting fully.
risk_rules.technician_notes: Instruct customer to try pushing inward on the door while operating the handle. If safe opens, remove excess items. Check bolt holes for debris.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Remove excess items from safe. Organize contents to leave clearance around bolt area. Check bolt holes for fallen objects.
risk_rules.customer_explanation: There's too much stuff inside the safe pressing against the door. Remove some items and organize what's left so nothing blocks the locking bolts.

risk_rules.likely_cause: The safe was dropped, struck, or experienced impact that activated the relocker device. This is a security feature that permanently locks the safe.
risk_rules.technician_notes: Inspect for signs of impact on safe exterior. Check relocker access point per manufacturer specs. Relocker must be drilled and disengaged before normal lock operation resumes.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Drill to access and disengage relocker device. Once open, inspect and replace relocker mechanism. Advise customer on safe placement to prevent future impacts.
risk_rules.parts_tools: Drill, carbide bits, relocker access template (manufacturer-specific), replacement relocker, borescope
risk_rules.customer_explanation: Your safe experienced an impact that triggered a built-in security lock. This is designed to protect contents if someone tries to break in. A technician must drill to disengage it and restore access.

risk_rules.likely_cause: The wiring connecting the keypad to the lock body has become loose, frayed, or disconnected from repeated door movement.
risk_rules.technician_notes: Check keypad cable connection at the lock body. Inspect wire insulation for damage where cable passes through door hinge area. Loose connectors can be reseated; damaged wires must be replaced.
risk_rules.recommended_action: Reseat keypad cable connector. If wires are damaged, replace keypad cable assembly. Secure cable routing to prevent future damage from door movement.
risk_rules.parts_tools: Replacement keypad cable, small flathead screwdriver, wire ties, multimeter for continuity testing
risk_rules.customer_explanation: The wiring between the keypad and the lock has come loose or been damaged. This is common from the cable flexing every time the door moves. Reseating or replacing the cable will fix it.
